milestone: Platform Foundation v1.0 — Enterprise Knowledge Graph live in production
phase: BarberOS current-state audit complete, and corrected. The repository was audited against the BarberOS brief and then checked against the live database -- in that order, which was the mistake: BarberOS is not in source control but IS installed and running in canonical production (mvvtngiopdrgiedjmhfb), across eleven migrations that no repository file contains. The platform foundation in this repo is genuinely strong and test-covered (860 unit tests passing, verified by running them), and the pieces BarberOS still needs are real: no booking data, no staff or second location, no appointment or availability model, no public API over the diagnostic results, nothing deployed and nothing able to send. The single most valuable next piece of work is bringing BarberOS into source control so it can be tested, reviewed and rebuilt -- applying nothing. READ-ONLY session: no code, no migrations, no deployments, nothing deleted.

Video Studio: a still image becomes a video, from inside the console. @hl-bos/video-studio finds the panels in a composite image by scoring every row and column for uniformity (a gutter is uniform along its length, artwork is not), plans a shot list of pans and zooms, and resolves that plan to exact rectangles at any millisecond; the Control Center's /video page records it to a real .mp4 in the browser with no account, no key and no upload. Verified end to end in headless Chromium against the CEO's own six-panel image: 6 panels found in a 3x2 grid, 8 shots, 16.7s, 1440x1416 MP4 of 7.3 MB that decodes and contains real frames. 62 unit tests. One real defect was found and fixed by that verification: the first cut cropped near-square comic panels to 16:9 and deleted the artist's caption bars, and the fix (contain-by-default framing) exposed a second bug where the renderer stretched instead of padding -- both now have regression tests that fail without the fix. Generated motion (a video model that animates the picture) is NOT built: the page names it, says what it would take, and shows no button for it.

Video Studio, second pass: the page told the CEO that generated motion needs a paid account, which is false and false in the expensive direction. Corrected: the provider panel now names the route that is genuinely our own (a freely licensed open model -- Wan, LTX -- on hardware we own, nothing metered, no image leaving our systems), states what every route costs in words about money, and is ordered cheapest-first. Status renamed needs-account -> not-built, because what is missing is the connection code, not the money. The console also now answers 'do I have an NVIDIA card?' itself, on the Video Studio page, rather than sending anyone to Device Manager -- it runs nvidia-smi, falls back to the Windows display-adapter list, distinguishes 'no card' from 'card with a missing driver', maps video memory to which models are actually runnable, and shows what it ran. The Windows branch cannot execute on the machine this was written on, so the whole decision is injectable and proved by five injected-probe tests; a mutation check confirmed they fail without the platform guard. Also fixed two shipped rendering defects found by reading the served HTML rather than the source: a sentence template that spliced a provider name into nonsense, and this toolchain dropping the space after a closing inline tag, which shipped the word 'notautomatically'.

The console can now RECEIVE work, not just send it. Until now the launcher could start the console but never update it, so once a copy of this repository was on the CEO's machine there was no way for finished work to reach him short of typing git commands -- the exact chore the operating contract forbids, and a hole left by every previous session including the one that wrote the launcher. scripts/update.mjs now runs on every start: it collects whatever has been finished since last time, reinstalls libraries if they changed, rebuilds if the code changed, then starts. It never destroys work (a folder with unsaved changes is left alone), never rewrites history (fast-forward only; a diverged folder stops and says so), never blocks startup (no network means one line and carry on), and never hangs on a credential prompt (GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0, so a private repo fails in seconds instead of freezing the launcher). Proved by scripts/local-test/verify-update.sh against real throwaway git repositories -- 7 git cases and 4 launcher-decision cases, all passing. One real batch defect was caught and fixed in the writing: `if A if B (X) else (Y)` binds the else to the inner if, so the first draft would have skipped the build entirely on a fresh clone and started a console that had never been built.

ATS Resume Optimizer: a working career tool, not a demo. @hl-bos/ats-resume parses a master resume and a job posting, builds an evidence matrix of every requirement against the candidate's own words, maps terminology (work stated in the posting's language, with the original detail and every number carried through), scores the fit on the owner's weighting and projects a second score that only counts revisions the evidence supports. apps/ats-resume-optimizer is the seven-screen app over it, with a split-screen review where every generated sentence discloses its source evidence, the requirement it answers and why it is worded that way. DOCX and PDF are generated from scratch (a ZIP/OOXML writer and a base-14 PDF writer, no document dependencies) and both round-trip: the text reads back out of the files we write. The central promise is enforced where the bytes are produced, not in the UI -- proved end to end against the running app by editing a bullet to an invented "$250M P&L across 14 countries", watching the validator name all three fabricated figures, and confirming the export dropped the line (X-Claims-Dropped: 1) while still writing the other eleven. Running it also found four real defects that reading the code had not: posting metadata ("Employment type: Full-time") being scored as an unmet requirement; a terminology rewrite that turned an $18M operating budget into "P&L ownership" (a P&L has a revenue line -- budget adjacency is now reported as a partial match with the difference spelled out); a splice-based rewrite producing broken English ("Cut warehouse and distribution operations, including dock dwell time by 27%"); and a stale-cache bug that served a previously exported document after an edit. Migration 0048 (ats, 17 tables) is written and verified against a local PostgreSQL 16 -- RLS enabled AND forced on all 17, 68 policies, zero anon grants, and the anti-fabrication CHECK constraints exercised -- and is UNAPPLIED to any project. No AI key is required: the built-in rules engine runs every feature, and Claude is an optional enhancement whose every suggestion is re-checked against the same evidence. The console can start it: a "Your software" panel on the Control Center home page shows whether it is running and starts it with one click, building first and waiting for a real health response before it reports success or offers a link -- the operating contract forbids telling the CEO to run a command, so "pnpm dev" was a feature request for the console, not an instruction for him.

BarberOS current-state audit, and the correction that followed. The audit searched this repository against the BarberOS brief and reported that BarberOS did not exist -- no app, package, schema, route or test -- with the word 'barber' appearing only as an industry taxonomy label in five files. That was correct about the repository and WRONG about the product. Reading the live database next showed BarberOS installed and running in canonical production: eleven migrations (0048_barberos_capability_catalog through 0058_barberos_client_crm) that are in no repository file, a barberos schema of 14 tables with RLS enabled and forced, a transform_audit schema of 10, 27 functions in each, and 17 public barberos_* RPCs. Two capabilities the audit had listed as MISSING are in fact built: client_rhythm/clients_due (learns a client's typical haircut interval and ranks who is overdue) and an owned-website builder with a real publish lifecycle. Revised completeness against the brief: about 35 percent, not 20-25, moving the workflow map from 1 EXISTS / 9 PARTIAL / 10 MISSING to 1 / 12 / 7. The honest limits matter as much: the client book is EMPTY (0 clients, 0 visits), the only shop is 'Herman Legacy Test Shop' with an unpublished site, transform_audit has NO public API so its 40 runs and 45 findings cannot be read by anything, and every one of those findings is confidence='inferred' with zero evidence URLs and a composite score of 0 -- the diagnostic has never actually fetched a website, because nothing is deployed and nothing has egress. No BarberOS code exists in this repository, so none of it is tested or reviewable here. Read-only throughout: nothing was created, altered, applied or deleted. docs/products/barberos/01-current-state-audit.md and 02-production-drift-map.md.

blockers.title: Production has drifted from the repository -- now measured exactly
blockers.meaning: This is no longer an estimate. Production holds 98 migrations; this repository holds 48. Fifty-four are applied in production and exist in no repository file; four are in the repository and have never been applied; sixteen more were applied under different version stamps than the files carry, which is the mechanical reason the protected one-click migration workflow cannot run. The number 0048 has been used by two unrelated migrations, so migration numbers no longer identify migrations. The important discovery: the fifty-four include the ENTIRE BarberOS product (eleven migrations, two schemas, twenty-four tables, fifty-four functions) plus two product lines nobody has documented -- dma_* (17 migrations, 28 tables) and jobscout_* (8 migrations, 8 tables) -- and one leftover object called temp_perftest_page_twin. None of it has a file, a test, a review or a rollback path. If that project were lost, nothing in this repository could rebuild it. Three questions only you can answer: where is the BarberOS application that calls those 17 RPCs (there is no client for them in source control); where did the 50 Western New York barbershop prospects come from (they were imported from a spreadsheet); and do the dma_* and jobscout_* lines still matter -- keep, export or retire? The fix is to bring the live schema back into source control as migrations that reproduce it exactly, with the pgTAP tests that should have come with them, applying nothing. That needs your go-ahead.
